prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I am looking for the photo that would make all the difference in my life. It’s very small and subject to fits of amnesia, turning up in poker hands, grocery carts, under the unturned stone. The photo shows me at the lost and found looking for an earlier photo, the one that would have made all the difference then. My past evades me like a politician. Wielding a fly-swatter, it destroys my collection of cereal boxes, my childhood lived close to the breakfast table. Only that photo can help me locate my fourteen lost children, who look just like me. When I call the Bureau of Missing Persons, they say, “Try the Bureau of Missing Photos.” They have a fine collection. Here’s one of Calvin Coolidge’s seventh wedding. Here’s one of a man going over a cliff on a dogsled. Here’s my Uncle Arthur the night he bought the prize peacock. O photo! End your tour of the world in a hot air balloon. Resign your job at the mirror-testing laboratory. Come home to me, you little fool, before I find I can live without you.

# The Photograph

I have been searching for a photograph for as long as I can remember—a small thing, really, barely larger than a playing card, its edges soft with handling, its colors faded to the sepia of old promises. I know that if I could just hold it again, everything would change. My life would click into place like a key turning in a long-rusted lock. But the photograph does not want to be found. It has a will of its own, a wanderer's heart, and it keeps turning up in places I never think to look: tucked inside a phone book in a city I've never visited, folded into the pocket of a coat I gave away a decade ago, pressed between the pages of a Bible in a motel room drawer. By the time I arrive, it has already left, as if it knows the exact rhythm of my pursuit and moves always one beat ahead.

The cruelest part is what the photograph shows. It is a picture of me, younger, searching for another photograph—an earlier one, more essential, more true. And that photograph, I understand now, depicts me searching for one before it, and so on, backward through time in a chain that has no beginning, only an infinite recession into smaller and smaller frames of longing. I am forever chasing myself chasing myself, each version a little more desperate, a little more certain that this next photograph, this one, will be the last one I ever need.

My past has noticed my search, and it does not approve. It has begun to fight back, quietly, viciously, in the manner of a thing that has decided it would rather not be found. My childhood cereal box collection—the one I kept in careful rows in the closet of my parents' house, Wheaties and Trix and Cap'n Crunch flattened and preserved like pressed flowers—has been destroyed. Not lost, not misplaced, but destroyed, as though some hand reached back through the years specifically to erase that particular joy. Report cards curl and blacken at the edges though no fire touches them. Home videos dissolve into static exactly at the moments I most want to rewatch. It is not decay. It is sabotage.

Eventually, worn down and desperate, I went to the Bureau of Missing Persons, thinking that surely an institution built for locating the lost could help me locate this small rectangle of my own history. The woman behind the counter listened to my description with the patience of someone who has heard every kind of grief, then shook her head slowly. "You want the Bureau of Missing Photos," she said. "Third floor. Follow the smell of old chemicals."

The Bureau of Missing Photos was a warren of gray filing cabinets stretching back farther than seemed architecturally possible, each drawer labeled in a code I couldn't decipher. The clerk there, a stooped man with developer-stained fingers, pulled out photograph after photograph for my inspection—a stranger's wedding day, an unidentifiable machine part, a dog mid-jump in a yard I did not recognize, a sunset over water that could have been any water anywhere. None of them were mine. None of them were even close. "These are all we have," the clerk said, not unkindly. "The one you want isn't the kind of thing that files itself where you'd expect."

I left empty-handed, as I always do.

Now I find myself reduced to something smaller than searching—to pleading. I whisper into the dark of my apartment, into the space behind the couch cushions, into the drawer where important things go to vanish, asking the photograph simply to come home. I no longer insist on understanding it, on holding it up to the light and finally seeing what earlier photograph it points to, what earlier one after that. I only want it back, the way you want a person back, the way you want to stop the leaving before you have to learn how to survive the empty space it leaves behind. Because that is the thing I fear most—not the search itself, endless as it is, but the day I finally stop searching. The day I look at the space where the photograph should be and simply learn, the way one learns anything terrible, to live without it.
outputs.L4:
# The Bureau of Missing Photos

I first heard about the photograph on a Tuesday that may have been a Thursday, from a woman who resembled my aunt but insisted she had never had a nephew, let alone one who resembled me. She said the photograph contained fourteen children standing in a field of wheat or possibly ash, and that I was somewhere in the background, slightly out of focus, holding the hand of someone whose face had already begun to fade even as the shutter clicked. She said if I found it, I would remember everything. If I did not find it, she implied, without quite saying so, that I would continue to be someone who merely resembled myself, forever.

This seemed like sufficient reason to begin looking.

The Bureau of Missing Photos occupied the seventh floor of a building that had six floors. I took the stairs, which spiraled in a direction stairs are not supposed to spiral, and arrived breathless in a waiting room filled with people holding empty frames up to their faces, checking their reflections in the glass as though the glass might, if patient enough, produce an image.

"I'm looking for a photograph," I told the clerk, a man whose name tag read APPROXIMATELY BURT.

"Everyone is looking for a photograph," Burt said, not unkindly. "Do you have a claim number?"

I did not have a claim number. I had a description: fourteen children, a field, myself in soft focus, the fading companion whose hand I held. Burt nodded as though this were a perfectly reasonable amount of information and led me through a door into a room containing several thousand filing cabinets, each labeled with a year that did not correspond to any calendar I recognized.

"We'll start with the substitutes," he said.

The first substitute was a photograph of a bowl of fruit. "This isn't it," I said.

"No," Burt agreed, "but notice the light. Very similar quality of light to what you're describing."

The second substitute showed fourteen adults, not children, standing in a parking garage. "Perhaps they grew up," Burt suggested, "and this is simply a later photograph of the same fourteen, taken after the one you want, which would mean the one you want still exists somewhere prior to this one, which is good news, temporally speaking."

I did not find this to be good news. I found it to be the kind of statement that made the floor feel less certain beneath me, the way all of Burt's statements did, each one a small erosion of whatever ground I thought I'd been standing on.

The third substitute was blank. Burt explained this was the most popular item in the archive, the one most frequently mistaken for the photograph everyone was looking for, precisely because it could be anything, and therefore felt, to the desperate mind, like it might be the one specific thing that mind required.

"I don't want anything," I said. "I want the one photograph. The one with the fourteen children and myself out of focus and the hand I was holding."

"Whose hand?"

"I don't remember. That's rather the point."

Burt considered this with the seriousness of a man considering a chess move that might end the game or might simply reset the board to its original position, no progress made, several hours lost. He opened another cabinet. Inside was a photograph of the waiting room I had just left, the people still holding their empty frames to their faces, except in the photograph, one of the frames contained an actual reflection, and the reflection was mine, and I was younger, and I was crying, though I could not remember, in this life, ever having cried in a room full of empty frames.

"Closer," Burt said, with something like professional satisfaction.

"It's not the one."

"No. But you'll notice progress."

I did not want progress. I wanted the photograph, entire and specific, the fourteen children and the field and the hand. I wanted to hold it and have it explain to me, wordlessly, the way photographs are supposed to, who I had been before I became someone who needed to ask.

We went on like this for what might have been an afternoon or might have been several years compressed into the shape of an afternoon, the way the Bureau seemed to compress and expand time according to some bureaucratic logic all its own. Substitute after substitute: a photograph of a door that led, Burt assured me, to a room where the real photograph was rumored to have once hung on a wall before the wall was demolished; a photograph of fourteen shadows with no bodies attached, which Burt found particularly promising, though I could not say why shadows without bodies should be more promising than any other configuration of proximate wrongness; a photograph, finally, of myself, alone, holding nothing, standing not in a field but in this very Bureau, taken, apparently, only moments before, though no one present had held a camera.

"You're getting warmer," Burt said, filing this last one away with the tenderness of a man filing away something he suspected was, in fact, the closest anyone had ever come.

I understood, somewhere in the recursive dimness of that afternoon-or-years, that I would not find the photograph. That the Bureau did not deal in finding, only in the elaborate, tender, endless process of not-quite-finding, of substitute after substitute arranged in such a way as to suggest an original that might, by this point, have never existed at all, or might exist so thoroughly, so saturated with meaning, that no actual photograph could ever satisfy it, could ever be anything other than a disappointment stapled to a memory.

Still, I would like it back. If whoever has it is reading this: I would like the photograph back, the one with the fourteen children and the field and myself out of focus and the hand I was holding, before I stop being able to specify what it is I am missing. Before the specific hardens into the general, into a bowl of fruit, into a blank rectangle that could be anyone's loss, into something Burt could file away with the satisfied murmur of *closer, closer,* while I forget, entirely, that I was ever looking for something with children in it, something with a field in it, something with my own face, faintly, barely, on the verge of appearing, if only the light would hold a moment longer, if only someone would stop asking me for a claim number I do not have and never will.

Before indifference. That's all I'm asking. Before the terrible, comfortable indifference that comes when even the search stops mattering, and every photograph looks, at last, exactly like every other one.
outputs.L5:
# The Wielding of the Only

There exists a peculiar power in the concept of "the only"—a phrase that carries within it both isolation and significance. To be the only one, or to possess the only means to achieve something, is to hold a position of singular importance in a world otherwise defined by abundance and repetition.

The act of wielding this uniqueness comes with tremendous responsibility. Consider the only witness to an event, the only key to a locked door, or the only person who understands a particular truth. In each case, the weight of exclusivity transforms an ordinary circumstance into something extraordinary. There is no redundancy to fall back on, no alternative path to pursue.

History remembers those who wielded singular power or singular knowledge, for better or worse. The only cartographer with a map to uncharted territory holds influence disproportionate to their physical strength. The only voice speaking truth in a room of silence carries a burden that many voices together would not bear.

Yet this wielding of "the only" is not always heroic or dramatic. Sometimes it manifests in quiet, everyday moments—the only friend who shows up, the only person who remembers a forgotten birthday, the only hand extended in a moment of need. These small acts of singular importance ripple outward, reminding us that being "the only" one to act is not a burden to fear, but an opportunity to matter.

In the end, the wielding of the only teaches us that scarcity itself can become a source of strength. When we recognize we are the only ones capable of a particular contribution, we are called not to shrink from that responsibility, but to rise to meet it—understanding that our uniqueness, however small the context, is never without consequence.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem about searching for a lost photograph that holds the key to understanding one's own past.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Photograph That Was Never Taken

Somewhere in the house that keeps rearranging itself while I sleep, there is a drawer that contains the photograph. I know this the way I know my own pulse—as a fact beneath facts, unprovable and absolute.

The drawer is sometimes in the kitchen, filed between the silverware and the sound of my mother's voice from 1987. Sometimes it lives inside the mirror, behind my reflection's reflection, in that thin country where light gets confused about which way to travel. Last Tuesday I found it inside a word I was trying to remember, the word itself a small wooden box that wouldn't open, though I could hear something shifting inside it like sand, like teeth, like years.

The photograph shows me standing in a doorway that doesn't exist in any house I've lived in, wearing an expression I've never made, holding the hand of someone whose face is a soft erasure, whose face is the exact shape of forgetting. Behind us: a yard becoming a highway becoming an ocean becoming the inside of my grandmother's throat when she sang.

I have searched for this photograph in the pockets of coats I no longer own. I have searched in the space between two heartbeats, where apparently entire decades can hide if they're patient enough. I have asked the moths, who know everything about eating light, and they only fold their wings like closing books and tell me to check the version of myself that exists three minutes before I was born.

Once, I found a photograph that was almost it—same doorway, same impossible yard—but I was facing the wrong direction, walking out instead of in, and the date stamped in the corner hadn't happened yet.

I keep searching anyway. Some nights the drawer sits in my own chest, right where the sternum makes its small white door, and I can feel it rattling with the specific gravity of an answer. If I could only find the right key, cut from the same metal as the moment I stopped being a stranger to myself—

But the key is also lost. The key may, in fact, be the photograph. Or the photograph may be a key shaped like a face, fitting a lock shaped like a question I haven't finished asking.

I go on searching. The house rearranges. The drawer waits, patient as sediment, holding the one image that would finally show me where I began—

if only it would stay in one place
long enough
to be found.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an absurdist, James Tate–style prose poem full of dark humor about the Bureau of Missing Persons and a missing photo.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Bureau of Missing Persons Regrets to Inform You**

I went to the Bureau of Missing Persons to report a missing photograph. The woman at the desk, whose name tag said HOPE though she seemed to be actively campaigning against it, asked me to describe the missing photo.

"It was of my grandmother," I said, "standing next to a horse that may or may not have been on fire."

"Was the horse missing too?"

"No, just the photo. The horse, as far as I know, continued about its business, whether that business was standing still or burning to death."

She wrote this down with the enthusiasm of a woman signing her own eviction notice. "Have you searched the usual places? Wallets. Shoeboxes. The pockets of coats you no longer own?"

I admitted I had not searched the pockets of coats I no longer owned, as this seemed to require a kind of time travel unavailable to me on a civil servant's schedule.

"We get a lot of this," she said. "Missing photographs. Missing socks. Missing years. Last week a man came in convinced his entire twenties had wandered off. We filed a report. We always file a report. It gives people something to hold, even if what they're holding is just a piece of paper confirming the shape of their loss."

I asked if the Bureau had ever actually found anything.

She looked at me the way you'd look at a child who asks if Santa pays taxes. "We found a man's dignity once. Under a bridge. It wasn't in great shape."

"And the photo?"

"The photo is gone," she said, not unkindly. "The photo has joined the horse. The horse has joined the fire, real or imagined. Everything joins something eventually. That's not a missing persons case. That's just Tuesday."

I left the Bureau without my photograph but with a form, stamped and official, stating that my grandmother, last seen standing next to a horse that may have been burning, was now considered a person of interest in her own disappearance. I keep the form in a drawer. Some nights I take it out and stare at it, the way you'd stare at the ash where a photograph used to be, waiting for the woman and the horse to step back out of whatever fire took them, waving, unburned, asking what all the fuss was about.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short surrealist flash fiction piece where the narrator obsessively searches for one photo among strange bureaucratic offices and bizarre images.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Photograph Office

I have been searching for the photograph since Tuesday, though the clerks insist Tuesday hasn't happened yet.

"You want Bureau 7," says the woman with the filing cabinet for a torso, drawers sliding open and shut where her ribs should be. Papers spill out like breath. "Third floor. Ask for Mr. Halloway. He collects the ones that got away."

Bureau 7 is underwater. Not flooded—underwater, entirely, fish drifting between desks in slow bureaucratic circles, wearing tiny spectacles, stamping documents with their tails. Mr. Halloway sits dry in the center of it all, a glass bell jar of air around his desk.

"The photograph," I tell him. "Me, age seven, standing in my grandmother's garden. There were sunflowers. I was laughing at something outside the frame."

"Everyone remembers the sunflowers," he says, not looking up. "No one remembers what was outside the frame. That's the trouble. That's always the trouble." He stamps a form. A fish salutes.

"Try Acquisitions," he says. "Fourth floor. Or possibly the parking garage. The building doesn't always agree with itself."

The parking garage is full of photographs instead of cars—thousands of them, propped upright, humming faintly like idling engines. I walk between rows of strangers' childhoods, someone's wedding day, a dog that died in 1987, all facing forward as if waiting to be driven somewhere.

None of them are mine.

A man in a valet's uniform made entirely of photo negatives approaches. His face develops and undevelops as he speaks. "Ticket?"

"I don't have a ticket. I'm looking for—"

"Everyone's looking for something outside the frame." He takes my hand and his fingers leave silver halide prints on my skin, tiny images of my own palm multiplying. "The photograph you want isn't lost. It's early. It hasn't happened yet, same as Tuesday."

"Then when will it happen?"

"When you stop being someone it could happen to."

I understand this the way you understand things in dreams—completely, and only for the duration of the understanding. Already it is leaving me, the way the garage is leaving me, the way the photographs turn their faces away one by one, embarrassed, as if I've asked to see something private.

Somewhere above me, floors and floors up, past Bureau 7 and its patient fish, I think I hear sunflowers.

I go back to searching. The building rearranges its hallways to accommodate me. This is, I understand, a kind of mercy.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a whimsical, melancholic prose poem that personifies a photograph as an elusive lover who keeps disappearing.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Photograph as Lover

You keep leaving me the way light leaves a room—slowly, then all at once, then not at all until I notice its absence and mourn what I didn't know I was losing.

I found you in a drawer that smelled of cedar and someone else's winters. You were wearing 1987 like a borrowed coat, squinting into a sun that no longer exists in that particular slant, that particular gold. I fell in love with the way you refused to age, the way you held your smile for thirty years without your jaw ever growing tired.

But you are a jealous kind of faithful. You let me hold you and still you slip away—into the crease that deepens each time I fold you into my pocket, into the fingerprint smudge that blurs your left eye like you're always about to wink and never quite arriving. I have lost you in bright rooms where the glare swallows your face whole. I have lost you in the dark, where you become only a rectangle of almost, a suggestion of someone I might have loved.

You promise nothing and I forgive you for it. This is the arrangement: I return to you like a tide, and you let me drown a little in what you almost say. Your silence is not cruelty. It is simply what happens when a moment is asked to last forever—it becomes shy. It becomes something that flinches from the very love that keeps it pinned to corkboard, to refrigerator door, to the inside cover of a book I'll forget I own.

Someday you'll yellow past recognition. Someday you'll be a ghost of a ghost, all your details dissolved into sepia rumor. I already grieve this future tense of you—the you that fades slower than memory but faster than stone.

Until then: I keep finding you and losing you in the same breath. I keep asking you to stay still, stay still, as if stillness were not the very thing that's killing you, silver and slow, in the small dark museum of my hands.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a piece of experimental literary fiction blending memory, loss, and absurd humor, ending with a direct address to an inanimate object.
counterfactuals.output:
# Notes Toward an Inventory of the Upright Freezer in My Mother's Garage, Two Years After

**1.**

The freezer hums in E-flat, or so my brother claims, though he has never once carried a tune and I suspect he made this up to have something to say at the funeral reception that wasn't *she's in a better place* or *at least it was quick*, which it was not, quick, not even a little, but that's a different document, filed under *Things We Agreed Not to Litigate*.

**2.**

Here is what I know about grief: it alphabetizes itself in your chest like a drawer of takeout menus, and you don't notice which language it's speaking until you try to order from it.

**3.**

An incomplete list of what is currently inside the freezer, compiled with a headlamp at 11 p.m. on a Tuesday because I could not sleep and the garage does not judge:

- Seven ice cube trays, none matching, one shaped like little smiling suns that she bought in 1994 and used exactly once because she decided smiling suns "made the whiskey look juvenile"
- A Cool Whip container (empty of Cool Whip; full of what I believe, based on smell and the handwriting on the masking tape, to be either chili or a homemade poultice for my father's knee, 2003)
- Freezer-burned Eggos, four boxes, purchased in what must have been a fugue state of extreme couponing
- A single pork chop, mummified, radiating the quiet dignity of an artifact in a museum no one visits
- My father's tackle box, which is not food, which someone put in here for reasons no living person can now explain, possibly to keep it from the ants, possibly out of grief-logic, which follows no known physics
- Three bags of peas, structurally unsound, more gravel than pea
- A Tupperware labeled DO NOT EAT — SCIENCE FAIR 1997 in my own eleven-year-old handwriting, contents unknown, opening it inadvisable, opening it eventually inevitable

**4.**

*Footnote, offered here because the essay format cannot hold what wants to be said sideways:* My mother did not believe in throwing food away. She believed, I think, that food thrown away was a kind of small failure, a crack in the dam of a house that otherwise ran, mostly, on the premise that nothing bad had ever really happened here, this house, these people, this family, though of course things had happened, terrible ordinary things, the way they happen everywhere, and the freezer filled up instead of the mouth, is what I'm trying to say. She fed the cold instead of speaking.

**5. Recipe Card, Found Taped to Freezer Door, Transcribed Verbatim**

> GRANDMA'S FREEZER JAM
> 4 c crushed strawberries
> 4 c sugar
> 1 pkg pectin
> stir until your arm wants to fall off honestly stir past that point too
> pour into containers, freeze, do not eat for one week, the waiting is the whole point, LISTEN TO ME, the waiting is the whole point

**6.**

We are not a family that talks about the dead directly. We talk about their appliances instead. "Remember how loud her blender was?" is code for *remember how loud she was, how present, how the whole house used to vibrate with her wanting things done a certain way, and now it doesn't, now it's so quiet you can hear the freezer, which is the only one of us still doing its job.*

**7. Aside, Possibly Unnecessary But I'm Leaving It In**

There was a period, roughly age nine to eleven, when I believed the freezer was a portal, specifically to Narnia, specifically because it was cold and large and my mother had told me, once, half-joking, "there's a whole world in there if you dig deep enough," meaning leftovers, meaning she'd lost track of what was in it, but I took this literally for two full years and would open the door sometimes just to check, breath fogging, waiting for snow, for fauns, for a lion with something useful to say about death, and getting instead a bag of freezer-burned peas staring back like a cataract.

I want to be clear: I do not think this was a waste of two years.

**8.**

The obituary said she "loved to cook for others." It did not say she once put an entire uncooked turkey in the chest freezer three weeks before Thanksgiving because she'd "gotten ahead of herself," and then forgot it was there, and bought a second turkey, and found the first turkey the following July, at which point she looked at me, dead serious, and said, "Well, we can't waste it," and I said "Mom it's July," and she said "The freezer doesn't know what month it is," which is, I now realize, the single truest thing anyone in my family has ever said about time.

**9.**

Here is a partial timeline of my mother's decline, reconstructed not from memory, which is unreliable, but from freezer contents, which are, apparently, forever:

- Item purchased in bulk, 2015 (she was still driving then, still went to Costco alone, still complained about the parking)
- Item purchased in bulk, 2017 (she'd started making lists on the backs of pharmacy receipts)
- Item purchased, unclear year, handwriting degraded into a long, exhausted scrawl I recognized only because I'd seen it on the hospital consent forms
- Nothing purchased after that. The freezer, like the rest of the house, stopped accumulating the future and became, simply, an archive.

**10.**

My brother wants to sell the house. I want to keep the freezer. We have not discussed how to keep a freezer without a house to plug it into, which is, I recognize, a metaphor so obvious it embarrasses me to write it down, and yet here I am, writing it down, because the alternative is not writing it down, and then what would I have?

**11.**

I opened the Science Fair Tupperware. I will spare you.

**12.**

Somebody has to say this plainly, so: I am not actually writing about a freezer. I am writing about the fact that she is not in the kitchen anymore, that no one is defrosting anything for Sunday, that the house has gone quiet in a way that has nothing to do with volume, and that I don't know what to do with my hands or my Sundays or the fourteen bags of frozen green beans that outlived her, so I am talking to an appliance instead, because it is large, and it is cold, and it is, unlike her, still right where I left it.

**13. Coda**

Dear freezer,

You kept everything. That was your one job and you did it with a diligence no one in this family could manage while alive. You held the pork chop past its usefulness, the peas past their pea-ness, the turkey past all reason, and you never once complained, never once said *this is too much, I am full, I cannot hold any more of what she couldn't bear to lose.*

I used to think you were a portal. I was wrong about the snow and the fauns, but maybe not about the rest of it — because here I am, headlamp still on, forehead nearly touching your frosted door, finding her in the handwriting on the masking tape, in the smiling-sun ice trays, in a jam she made me promise to wait a whole week for.

I'm going to keep you plugged in as long as I can. I know that's not sustainable. I know a house is coming down around you and a truck is coming to haul you to some other garage, some smaller life, some outlet that may or may not accept your particular hum.

But right now, tonight, you are the last machine in this family still doing the one thing we could never manage:

holding on to what we couldn't say, and not asking us, even once, to explain why.
